title: Remote access: what is being granted?
basic: Remote access can provide a terminal, desktop, file transfer, application session or routed network path. These grant different capabilities and require different controls.
intermediate: Draw client, identity provider, gateway and target resource. Separate transport reachability, authenticated identity and permitted operations.
advanced: Choose the narrowest access needed for the job. A successful VPN connection must not automatically grant administrator rights or access to every internal service.
practice: Compare an SSH terminal, RDP desktop and application gateway in a worksheet: user, target, operation, authentication and revocation.

title: SSH: encrypted terminal and server identity
basic: SSH provides encrypted remote sessions and additional channels such as file transfer or forwarding when permitted by the server.
intermediate: Verify the server host-key fingerprint through a trusted independent channel. User authentication and host authentication solve different problems.
advanced: Investigate an unexpected host-key change; do not routinely delete known-host entries or disable checking. Limit server reachability and permitted account actions.
practice: The supplied SSH configuration points only to a separately configured loopback lab server on port 2222. Its inspection command does not connect.

title: Keys, passwords, MFA and credential handling
basic: A public key can be authorized by a server; the corresponding private key must remain protected. A host key identifies a server, while a user key authenticates a client.
intermediate: Use individual identities, protect private keys and use appropriate passphrases or hardware-backed credentials. Plan MFA or other additional checks where the access platform supports them.
advanced: Agent forwarding exposes use of the agent through another host and should not be enabled by default. A key pair is not automatically MFA, and an SSH key does not expire unless the surrounding policy implements expiry or certificates.
practice: Inventory who can use each lab account and how access is revoked. Never put passwords or private keys into shared command examples.

title: RDP, VNC and graphical sessions
basic: Remote desktop tools expose an interactive graphical session. Clipboard, device and drive redirection can move data across the session boundary.
intermediate: Verify the server identity, allowed users and resource redirection policy. Use supported clients and the intended gateway or VPN path. Authentication features differ between implementations.
advanced: Network Level Authentication performs authentication before a full RDP session is established; it is not the same as MFA. VNC protection depends on the implementation and configuration.
practice: Use a separately configured owned Windows lab host. Check denied accounts and unnecessary clipboard/drive access as well as a legitimate login; no RDP or VNC service is enabled by this book.

title: VPNs: encryption, routes and access policy
basic: A VPN creates a protected path between peers or networks. Routing determines which traffic uses it; firewall and application rules still determine permitted access.
intermediate: Compare split tunneling with full tunneling. Document DNS behavior, IPv4 and IPv6 routes, endpoint trust and the intended internal destinations.
advanced: WireGuard peer AllowedIPs participates in destination selection and accepted source-address checks; it is not an application authorization rule. Route installation also depends on the client or helper configuration.
practice: Review an approved WireGuard or OpenVPN profile with the administrator. Test one allowed service and one denied service; a handshake alone is not proof of correct policy.

title: Bastions, jump hosts and access gateways
basic: A bastion provides an intermediate access point; an application gateway may authorize access to individual resources rather than a whole network.
intermediate: Document which identities may reach the gateway and which targets they may access afterward. Restrict outbound access from the gateway and protect its administration.
advanced: A jump host adds a boundary but does not remove the need to verify the final host or protect credentials. Centralization can simplify auditing while concentrating availability and compromise risk.
practice: Draw user -> gateway -> selected server. Evaluate both gateway compromise and gateway outage; define how access can be revoked and recovered.

title: SSH local forwarding: follow both endpoints
basic: A local SSH forward accepts a connection on the client and carries it through SSH to a destination reached from the SSH server.
intermediate: Bind the client listener to loopback when only the client needs it. Confirm the server permits forwarding and the destination is explicitly approved.
advanced: The destination 127.0.0.1 is evaluated on the SSH server side, not necessarily on the client. Forwarding changes reachability; it does not add application authentication. Avoid forwarding unintended management services.
practice: The workbook maps client port 8899 to a fictional HTTP service on server-side port 8910. ExitOnForwardFailure checks forward setup, not every later destination connection.

title: Remote file transfer and integrity
basic: SFTP transfers files through SSH. Its permissions and path access still depend on the remote account and server policy.
intermediate: Verify host identity and use a dedicated lab folder with synthetic files. Decide which transfers are allowed and protect sensitive local outputs.
advanced: A transfer success does not prove provenance. Compare an independently trusted digest when integrity matters. Restrict accounts to required paths and operations where supported.
practice: Use the supplied SFTP command only after configuring the local SSH lab. Compare a permitted file operation with an explicitly denied path.

title: Least privilege, logging and revocation
basic: Remote access should be attributable to an individual and limited in resource, privilege and duration. Service identities require their own scoped policy.
intermediate: Record session starts, authentication outcomes, target resource and administrative changes without logging reusable secrets. Define approval and expiry for temporary access.
advanced: Disabling an account or key may not terminate an already established session. Revoke credentials and active sessions according to the platform, and verify the result.
practice: Test login denial after revocation and separately test whether an existing lab session remains usable. Document idle timeouts, absolute limits and emergency recovery procedures.

title: Diagnose remote access one layer at a time
basic: Distinguish name resolution, route, transport connection, host verification, user authentication and resource authorization. Each has different evidence.
intermediate: Check the intended endpoint and port, local route and server listener before changing authentication settings. Preserve useful error messages while redacting personal details.
advanced: A timeout is not proof of a wrong password. Permission denied after a completed SSH handshake is different from a refused TCP connection. Do not weaken certificate or host-key validation to hide a configuration error.
practice: Use SSH verbose output in a controlled lab, noting that it can reveal paths and identifiers. Retest both intended access and explicitly denied access after a repair.
